rows.en: A great work concerning the language of Holy Scripture is ascribed to the first generations of the Scribes, namely: their correction of the script and of the language. As to the script, we are told that Ezra changed the script in which the Torah was originally written. For it was originally written in the Hebrew script, and Ezra came and wrote it in the Assyrian script (Sanhedrin 21b). The account of these matters is founded on an old tradition, held firm in all generations, and we have no compelling reason to cast doubt on this tradition. The sages in the Talmud wondered at the matter from various sides, but they did not cast doubt on it, for the event was verified in their eyes. They did, however, seek to find a support for the permission to change the script. On this one of the sages (R. Eliezer ben Jacob) adds that one of the prophets who came up with them from the exile testified to them that the Torah should be written in Assyrian (Zevaḥim 62b). This is like an explicit apology for Ezra's daring to change the script: he made the matter depend on the power of prophecy of the prophets who came up with them, on whose word Ezra did what he did. Other sages tried to devise another apology, by proving the permission — by their ways of midrash — from Scripture (Sanhedrin 22a). That these later sages turned away from the tradition of R. Eliezer ben Jacob, although they said of him that his Mishnah is “a kav, but clean,” and tried to make the matter depend on their midrash and to prove that the permission to change the script is already hinted at in Scripture, is no doubt because it did not suit them to make the matter depend on prophecy; for they found it hard to believe that the prophets permitted writing in Assyrian, since a prophet is not permitted to introduce anything new from now on. Now we know very well that these apologies are weak, but the core of the matter is clear: it is an old tradition that Ezra changed the script from Hebrew to Assyrian. From then on they wrote the Torah in the Assyrian script and left the Hebrew to the hedyotot [common people]. This came from their wish to give the holy writings an added holiness; therefore they ordained that it should have a script of its own, while for every common use they had the old Hebrew script. Indeed they left it also to the hedyotim, that is, the Kutim [Samaritans], whom they called by the nickname “hedyotim.” For the Torah of the Kutim is written in the Hebrew script to this day. Accordingly we find that the script on the coins struck by the Hasmoneans was not the Assyrian script, for they did not use it for any common thing; the script on those coins was Hebrew. And if we look at it carefully, we find that it is exactly like the script of the Kutim. Now the reason why Ezra and his company changed the script from Hebrew to Assyrian was twofold. First, the reason lay in the change of the times. For just as during the days of the exile they learned the language spoken by the peoples among whom they lived, so no doubt they also learned their script, as clearly follows from the words of the Talmud that the Assyrian script came up with them from Assyria (Sanhedrin 21b; Yerushalmi Megillah 1:11). But they had yet another reason for this, namely to widen the separation between the Jews and the Samaritans, that is, the Kutim, and to make a visible mark distinguishing the Torah of the Jews from the Torah of the Samaritans.{v1_04_11:1} For the Kutim themselves wrote their Torah in the Hebrew script, although Assyrian was the script of their land; for their copy of the Torah came from a time earlier than this, before Ezra changed the script, and therefore they held on to the script in which they had received the copy of the Torah. And the masters of the Talmud rightly conjectured that they left the Hebrew script to the Kutim; and no doubt their intent is that they left them this script in the copy of their Torah. By this Ezra also did a great thing for the preservation of the correct and true text. For it could easily happen that Jews would copy from a Samaritan Torah scroll, and who would stand surety for them that they would not falsify or corrupt the readings, as in fact in the course of time [the Samaritans] falsified the Torah in many places? Therefore Ezra did well to change the script; it became a dividing screen between the Jews and the Kutim and served them as a safeguard to keep them from every stumbling.

Yet not only with regard to the script but also with regard to the language did the Scribes make corrections, to set the readings of the Torah right. These corrections are called tikkunei soferim [corrections of the Scribes]. Of particular corrections — in which place, and what it was that they corrected — no clear word has reached us. The ancients already groped in the dark in this matter, and the eighteen places in Scripture that they pointed out, which in their opinion the Scribes corrected (Mekhilta and Tanḥuma, Be-shallaḥ; Genesis Rabbah ch. 49; Leviticus Rabbah ch. 11; and in many places), are nothing but a slight conjecture; and in most of the places where they thought another wording would have been fitting, we find that the correct one, by the plain sense of Scripture, is as it stands before us in Scripture, and it is not a correction made by the Scribes (Ibn Ezra on Numbers 11:15). But the core of the matter is clear: the Scribes made corrections in Scripture, and these were called tikkunei soferim. Moreover, in all the Torah scrolls in our hands there are hints of corrections by means of dots above some words of the Torah. These dots were ascribed to Ezra. The masters of aggadah said of them that some words in the Torah were doubtful to him, and he did not want to lay a hand on the readings before him; he left them as they were and put dots over them to give a hint of the doubt (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 34; Numbers Rabbah ch. 3). It is true that these dots are very old. For we find that the great sages who lived in the first century after the destruction expounded their midrashim on these dots, and this is proof that they held them to be very ancient. From all this we see in any case that from of old the opinion spread among the people that the Scribes made corrections in the Torah; and further, that where a doubtful reading lay before them they made marks, namely the dots, to hint at the doubt. Hence of necessity they believed that in the time of the Scribes, when [the Scribes] strove to restore the Torah to its former state, they found readings of which some were corrupt and some doubtful. And it should not seem strange to us that the ancient sages thought the books had become corrupt in the course of time, although the Torah was set in order and kept in the Temple of the Lord. For we know the fate of the Torah scroll in the days of King Josiah son of Amon, and we have heard the complaint of the prophet Jeremiah against the wise men of his generation, when he said: “How do you say: We are wise, and the Torah of our God is with us? But behold, the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie” [Jeremiah 8:8].⚠1 We are also told that even after the time of the Scribes, when the books were surely kept with excellent care, they nevertheless found in the Temple court scrolls with differing readings, so that they themselves were in doubt which was the right one and which the spoiled one; and they did not decide from tradition, but because they found the one reading in two scrolls they upheld it, and the other they found in only one scroll and set it aside (Soferim ch. 6). Also, many readings in our books do not have the agreement of the sages of the Talmud, since we see that these sages had readings on which they based their expositions, and these differ from the Masorah. Is there not an endless number of variants in the readings of Scripture between the books of Babylonia and the books of the Land of Israel? And although already in a very early time they occupied themselves with matters of the Masorah and with fixing the text of Scripture, it is nevertheless clear that at all times there were various readings in our holy books; and this very fact, that already in ancient days they weighed and searched with great effort to examine the readings, to sift them and to purify them, surely proves that their time needed it. How then can we wonder if the sages thought that in the time of the Scribes, before which there was a time of forgetting and neglect of the Torah, this neglect caused corruption of the books, so that the Scribes were compelled to make corrections and to restore the matter to its former state? But what these corrections of the Scribes were, of this no clear word has reached us. Only by way of conjecture can one penetrate the secret of this tradition. We should pay attention to two expressions brought in the Talmud, namely miqra soferim and ittur soferim. The masters of the Talmud explain the sense of these expressions in a strange way, and in a manner from which it appears that their sense was hidden from them and that they groped in the dark. The expression miqra soferim was understood by them as the correct reading of the words. This reading was handed down to us by the early ones, who were called Soferim (Nedarim 37b, in the Ran); they did not invent a new reading, but taught them the correct manner of reading as it had been in the first generations, back to Moses at Sinai (ibid.). They were compelled to this instruction because their time was a time of decline of the language, so that many did not know how to read a book, and even among those who knew, the reading of the words had surely become corrupt; therefore their first work was to clear these thorns from the language and to correct the reading — not as they invented it from their own heart, but the reading as it had been in the ancient generations. But a thing of such slight value as this is self-evident, and to mention it is superfluous. We cannot believe that they preserved for us in such an explicit expression a thing that is self-evident; even if it had not been preserved for us in tradition, no man of understanding would doubt it — while we see, on the other hand, that the most ancient ones hid from us many great and precious things and said nothing about them. Therefore the expression miqra soferim must of necessity be understood of another matter.{v1_04_13:1} Still more obscure is the expression ittur soferim. What is this ittur, and what is its sense and nature? Shall we understand by it that at times superfluous words were written to beautify the language, and it was called ittur [ornament] because it adorns the language by this? Or shall we say the opposite, that the sense of the word ittur is removal, and its meaning would be that at times letters that ought to have been put in the words were removed from them (the first explanation is that of the Ran and the second that of the Rosh)? But whether we say this or that, it is impossible that the word soferim refers to the ancient teachers [mevinim]. For if it referred to them, and they added words for the beauty of the language or omitted letters that ought to be there, it would not be right to say that they changed nothing but that such was the tradition — is not the ittur ascribed to the Scribes? Therefore of necessity ittur soferim does not refer to the particular Scribes, that is, the teachers in the days of Ezra and after him, but refers to the ornament for the beauty of the language that was customary among writers in general. But this too is very far from the truth, and we cannot believe it, for two reasons. First, from the form of the expression it is clear that it refers to the particular Scribes, and the expression soferim is not found with another sense. Second, for what purpose would one need to mention that all the turns of phrase that serve the beauty of the language, or what was removed for the sake of its grammar, all came from the pen of the writer of the Torah — and who ever doubted this? Some of the sages after the Talmud already sensed that the word soferim in the expression ittur soferim has no other sense than the particular Scribes. They said explicitly that in the time before the Scribes the common people corrupted some words by adding some letter in their reading, and the Scribes came and removed the letter and commanded to read without the letter; but they did not do so on their own judgment, but because they had a tradition to that effect (*Arukh*, s.v. ʿ-ṭ-r). But we are not told how they found the matter written in the Torah. If it was written without the letter that the corrupters added in their reading, and was written in the correct reading, in agreement with the reading of the Scribes, and the Scribes taught the people to read properly and as it is explicitly written — what particular work is this, that they specified it and ascribed it to the Scribes? Is it not also included in miqra soferim? In short, these two expressions are closed and sealed, and all that is said about them in the Talmud does not help us to remove the darkness from them.

1.he: ותורת אלהינו עמנו אכן הנה לשקר עשה עט שקר סופרים
1.note: Weiss quotes the verse loosely; Jeremiah 8:8 reads ותורת ה' אתנו. Kept his wording.

rows.en: Yet this we cannot deny in any way: the expressions tikkunei soferim, miqra soferim and ittur soferim are very old expressions, and they tell us of the different works that the Scribes performed. About the work of the corrections it is very hard to say anything clear, because before us the corruption is already corrected and we cannot know in which place the corruption was; and as for our finding that the masters of the Talmud in the midrashim count and number all the places that the Scribes corrected, we have already seen that their words have only the value of aggadah. Yet it is true that the Scribes made various corrections to purify the readings from corruptions that had come upon them in the course of time. And it is very likely that tikkunei soferim is a general term that includes all kinds of corrections in Holy Scripture, and its particular kinds are miqra soferim and ittur soferim. For miqra soferim is nothing other than a kind of the corrections they made by adding words for a better understanding; but they did not add them in writing, only in reading, and therefore they called such corrections miqra soferim [the reading of the Scribes]. Likewise ittur soferim is a kind of the corrections they made by removing written words; but they did not erase them from the writing, they removed them only in thought and commanded that they be read in a manner other than what is written before us. This conjecture finds its confirmation if we consider carefully that old saying which speaks of these expressions. When R. Isaac says: “Miqra soferim, ittur soferim, words read and not written, and words written and not read, are a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai,” will not every man of understanding see from the measure of these words that the expressions miqra soferim, ittur soferim, read and not written, written and not read, were not invented by the speaker, but were old expressions, known and famous, which are names for works of the Scribes, and that the speaker only added an explanation of them according to his opinion? But we have already seen that his explanation has no foundation or root. Yet the expressions need an explanation only if they are understood as four kinds of corrections that the Scribes made. But it is close to the truth that this is not so, and that we have here only two kinds of their corrections together with their explanations, namely miqra soferim and ittur soferim: the explanation of miqra soferim is “read and not written,” and the explanation of ittur soferim is “written and not read.” But they corrected only in the reading and not in the writing, because even according to what is written the sense of the matter is not lacking; only by their correction they brought it about that the saying has a clearer sense, and their correction is like an explanation of Scripture. And if the masters of the Talmud ascribe all these corrections to a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai, we do not know their intent in this; but this we know, that it is impossible to say that the writer of the Torah delivered the words as they are written before us and commanded that they not be read as they are written but in another manner, for this is a thing that sound reason cannot bear. How shall we say that Moses wrote a word in the Torah whose sense in the saying we do not know,⚠1 and commanded that it be read in the fitting manner — why did he not write it properly at once? And even if we could appease our mind by saying that he had a hidden intent that is concealed from us, what shall we say about the “written and not read” and the “read and not written” in the rest of the holy writings? Shall we say of these too that there is a secret and a hidden intent in them? And even if we wish to concede even this strange thing, and to say that the prophets who wrote their words in a book also had a concealed intent in changing the written text from the fitting reading, how can we find any opening for argument in those writings which, according to the opinion of the sages of the Talmud, were not written in a book by their authors, but others wrote them according to what they had received? Surely these of necessity received the text as it ought to be read, for so they had heard it; why then do we find in these books most of these changes? Therefore it seems clear that these corrections came from the hand of the Scribes; they made them and established them for the benefit of a clear understanding of the holy writings. A third kind of corrections the Scribes made: at times they corrected the written text and commanded that some word be read otherwise than we find it written, from their wish to speak in clean language.{v1_04_14:1} Of this kind also is the change in the reading of some word which, if read as written, could lead the reader into error in the belief in corporeality. This is found especially where Scripture speaks of man seeing God, as in “Three times in the year shall all thy males appear before the Lord God” [Exodus 34:23], and many like it, where no doubt it was originally written and read yir'eh [shall see], and not yera'eh [shall appear] as it is pointed in our books. For if it were so, it would not be fitting to say et penei Elohim, but el penei Elohim. Therefore it is very likely that the Scribes changed the reading in order to keep away the belief in corporeality.{v1_04_14:2} Yet in all these kinds of corrections the reason was not that the books had become corrupt, but that they too thought that the written reading was the reading that existed originally, only they changed its reading for one of the reasons we have stated. But no doubt they also found readings which in their opinion were corrupt, and nevertheless they did not change their writing but changed the reading. This was where the corrupt word could be explained without any correction; yet because in their opinion the word is explained by their correction in a clearer and more ample manner, they did not refrain from correcting it; but they did not correct it in the written text, they corrected only its reading. Of this kind are many of the “written and not read” that we find in Scripture.{v1_04_15:1} But not all the “written and not read” arose from the corruption of the readings before the time of the Scribes, for many of them arose in the time after the Scribes, down to a very late time, and only through the fault of the copyists. For this reason we find various variant readings that the masters of the Talmud and the midrashim had, against the Masorah. And in the Targums we find that at times they translated according to the ketiv, but mostly according to the qeri; and this is a sign that many of the variant readings are later than the ancient Targums. And who knows whether some of the corrections in the Masorah that were made by changing the reading did not have their root in the ancient Targums, that is, that the masters of the Masorah corrected the reading against the ketiv according to them? Now we see that most of the kinds of corrections that we have ascribed to the Scribes have the character of interpretation, and we can judge in part from their nature that precision in expressions and words was already the essence of their interpretations and explanations of the holy writings.

footnotes.en: See my book *Mishpat Leshon ha-Mishnah* (Vienna 1867), where I inquired at length into the rules of the language of the Mishnah, and where I cited all the authors of our time and before it who wrote their inquiries on the grammar of this language. On the decline of the old Hebrew language and the spoiling of its beauty in the exile, see the introductions to Holy Scripture, and especially Gesenius in the *History of Holy Scripture*,⚠1 p. 28 ff.; de Wette⚠2 in his inquiries into the science of introduction, p. 67; Hartmann in his introduction to the book of Ecclesiastes; and Hävernick in the introduction to his commentary on the book of Daniel.

So too is the matter with the script; and therefore R. Eliezer ben Jacob said that the prophets testified, and not that they permitted.⚠3

footnotes.en: See Rashi on Nedarim at the place mentioned, who explains nothing about the word soferim; it seems that he explains the word soferim as the reading of teachers in general, that is, the customary and usual reading. Likewise he does not explain, about ittur soferim, what is meant by the word soferim; and perhaps he too understood it in the way we wrote in the text, and not of the particular Scribes. The Rosh also explains nothing at all about the word soferim, and the Tosafot do not explain it either. But I have already shown in the text that there is no doubt about this, that the intent is clearly the ancient Scribes. So too the Ran understood it in his explanation of miqra soferim, and so the explanation of the *Arukh* on ittur soferim. Whoever considers the words of R. Isaac there in the Gemara will easily find that he was not the inventor of these expressions, but they were very old and he explains them. And because they refrained from deciding that the books had become corrupt at any time, they tried to explain these expressions in various directions by way of aggadic midrash; and so he explained that all of it is a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai. But for the purpose before us such explanations have no power to bring us out of the confusion, because of the contradictions in them, and also because this is no foundation on which we can build in our inquiry into antiquities.
